v.q: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a system must choose between which two properties?
o: Consistency and availability
Consistency and partition tolerance
Availability and low latency
Durability and throughput
v.w: Partitions happen, so partition tolerance is not optional. The real choice during one is consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (answer, possibly stale).

v.q: Which statement about CAP is NOT true?
o: A system can give up partition tolerance and stay safe on a real network
During a partition you choose consistency or availability
Partitions happen in real networks
CP systems may refuse some requests
v.w: Real networks partition, so partition tolerance is not optional. The choice is between C and A.

v.q: A bank's ledger node cannot reach the other replicas. It rejects writes until the partition heals. Which choice is this?
o: CP: it chooses consistency over availability
AP: it chooses availability over consistency
Neither, since this is simply a bug
Eventual consistency between replicas
v.w: Rejecting requests to avoid divergent data is the CP trade-off. AP systems keep serving and reconcile later.

v.q: A cache of exchange rates keeps answering during a network split, even though some values are stale. Which choice is this?
o: AP: availability over consistency
CP: consistency over availability
A violation of CAP
A bug in the replication
v.w: Answering with possibly stale data is the AP trade-off, acceptable for rates that change slowly.

v.q: A client calls a payment service and the request times out. What can the client conclude?
o: Nothing for sure, the payment may or may not have happened
The payment definitely failed, so retry freely
The payment definitely succeeded, so do nothing
The network is down and the client can stop
v.w: This is why retries need idempotency keys. Without one, a retry can charge twice.

v.q: A payment API call times out. Which reaction is safe?
o: Retry with the same idempotency key
Assume it failed and retry with a new key
Assume it succeeded and do nothing
Show the user a success page
v.w: The outcome is unknown, so the retry must be safe to repeat. The same key lets the server detect a duplicate.

v.q: What does an idempotent operation guarantee?
o: Repeating it has the same effect as doing it once
It is guaranteed to succeed on the first try
It always runs in constant time
It is never retried by clients
v.w: `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition. `POST` is not, so add an idempotency key for payments.

v.q: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by definition?
o: POST
PUT
DELETE
GET
v.w: POST can create a new resource each time, so payments need an idempotency key.

v.q: Why can't you rely on wall-clock timestamps from different servers to order events?
o: Clocks drift and are never perfectly synchronised
Timestamps are too large to store in a database
Servers always run in different time zones
Only databases are allowed to keep a clock
v.w: Use logical clocks, version vectors or a single sequencer when order matters. Even NTP leaves skew of milliseconds or more.

v.q: Which tool orders events across servers without trusting wall clocks?
o: A logical clock or version vector
The server system time
The request timeout
The log file size
v.w: Logical clocks capture causal order without depending on synchronised hardware clocks.

v.q: Quorum reads and writes (R + W > N) are used to:
o: Any read overlaps at least one replica with the latest write
Writes become faster than reads on every node
Replication is no longer needed for durability
A leader is elected without any voting
v.w: With N=3, W=2 and R=2 the read and write sets always share a node, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write.

v.q: With N=5 replicas, which choice guarantees that a read sees the latest acknowledged write?
o: W=3 and R=3
W=2 and R=2
W=1 and R=1
W=2 and R=3
v.w: R + W must exceed N, so read and write sets overlap. 3 + 3 = 6 > 5.

v.q: What problem does consensus (Raft, Paxos) solve?
o: Getting several nodes to agree on a value despite failures
Compressing the traffic between data centres
Encrypting messages before they are sent
Balancing HTTP requests across web servers
v.w: Coordination services like etcd and ZooKeeper use consensus for leader election, configuration and locks.

v.q: Which job is NOT a typical use of a consensus system such as etcd or ZooKeeper?
o: Storing bulk order data
Leader election
Distributed locks
Shared configuration
v.w: Consensus stores are small and strongly consistent. They are not meant for bulk data.

v.q: A leader is elected and then loses connectivity, while a new leader takes over. What mechanism stops the old leader from corrupting data?
o: Fencing tokens or epochs that storage rejects when stale
Hoping the old leader notices the change soon
Using longer timeouts on every client
Restarting every client in the cluster
v.w: Each election increments a number. Storage refuses writes carrying an older number, so a zombie leader cannot win.

v.q: A paused leader wakes up and tries to write with an old epoch number. What does storage do?
o: It rejects the write
It accepts the write as the newest
It merges the write with the new leader's
It restarts the new leader
v.w: Storage compares the token with the latest one it has seen and refuses stale holders.
